text:
Norman Swan: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, vitamin D supplements and your heart. Another win for
keyhole surgery in women. How things are changing in the resuscitation of
newborn babies in the labour ward, and also in the care of preterm babies. And
jogging and your back.

Most people will suffer an episode of back pain some time in their lives, often
more than one. It's a huge cause of lost days at work and medical costs, not to
mention the disability that can be involved. You can find experts who say that
jogging is poison for the back because it pummels the spine. But a world first
study from Deakin University on the effects of jogging and running on
intervertebral discs suggests otherwise. The lead author is Daniel Belavy and
he's in our Melbourne studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Daniel Belavy: Good evening Norman.

Norman Swan: So tell us about this study.

Daniel Belavy: Well, as you introduced, back pain is a massive problem for
Australian society, and it's the leading cause of disability and lost productivity in
the country, even when you account for more deaths due to other diseases. And
in managing this sort of issue, what I wanted to look at was to see can we find
ways to, for example, strengthen the discs in the back. And the conventional
wisdom in the research field is that either you can't or if there is an effect, that it's
going to be too slow to have a meaningful effect in a person's life.

Norman Swan: And whilst there was some evidence in animals, there was no
evidence in humans that exercise did make a difference.

Daniel Belavy: Precisely, and the thing is that what might happen or be relevant
in an animal mightn't be the case in humans because…

Norman Swan: And we're talking about the shock absorbers between the
vertebra, the bones in the spine.

Daniel Belavy: Precisely, yes, and as you said, this research has been done
with animals before, but their metabolism is a lot faster and also they walk on all
fours. And whether that applies then to humans is another matter.
 
Norman Swan: So tell us what you did in the study?

Daniel Belavy: Well, what I decided to do is to look at certain kinds of physical
activity that we think are possibly going to be at the very worst not detrimental to
the spine at high volumes, or they might be beneficial. Based upon the work from
animals and also from other studies we've seen before, I thought that examining
walking or running might be a good way to see if this exercise can actually
improve the discs.

Norman Swan: So you have three groups of relatively young people, 25, 35,
men and women, with varying levels of activity. Tell us about their varying levels
of activity.

Daniel Belavy: Well, we had obviously a group of people who didn't do any sport
at all, they were healthy, they had no back problems at all, but they just were
simply not involved in any regular physical activity. And then we had a group of
people who regularly run marathons, so running at least 50 kilometres a week
and doing that for at least five years. And also a group of people who were
regular joggers, so running 20 to 40 kilometres a week, and also for at least five
years, but also, again, no other kind of sports. We just looked at people who just
ran. So triathletes and so forth we didn't look at.

Norman Swan: And you did MRIs on their backs?

Daniel Belavy: Yes.

Norman Swan: What did you find? So this is not a randomised trial, this is just
seeing what the effect was.

Daniel Belavy: Just seeing what the effect was, because there is no data in
humans, before you go off and do the randomised controlled trial you need to
see if there is any kind of effect at all, and back in the studies on bone in the late
'80s and early '90s you needed that first cross-sectional study between different
types of sports or different types of athletic groups to see if there was a
difference, and that was then the justification to say, okay, let's go off and do a
randomised controlled trial.

Norman Swan: So what did you find about their discs?
 
Daniel Belavy: Well, we found that the runners had better discs. And most
interestingly, on the one hand we found there was more water and more
hydration in the disc, and that's an indicator of a healthier disc. And we also
found in the marathon runners, and I was personally really, really surprised about
this finding, that their discs were actually bigger. Compared to the size of their
bones in the spine, the discs were a lot bigger, and that's an indicator that the
discs actually got bigger in response to the loading.

Norman Swan: And this is controlled for because your muscles around the spine
are going to be stronger and so on…

Daniel Belavy: Well, not necessarily, the muscles, actually there was no
difference between the different groups in their muscle size.

Norman Swan: And so this is a pure effect on…but I thought there wasn't that
much difference between the joggers and the long distance runners?

Daniel Belavy: There wasn't much of a difference between the two, that's true,
and that did surprise me a little bit, I thought we might see a stepwise effect, but
looking at the data further, it seemed like…sometimes you hit a ceiling with how
much of a response you can get from a tissue. Like, you can do muscle training
as much as you want, you only get so far, no matter how much you train your
muscle, it won't keep on expanding and keep on getting bigger.

Norman Swan: So why this effect then? So basically healthier, larger discs with
jogging and running, and 150 minutes a week I think is what you said with the
jogging roughly. So what was causing it? Was it the impact or what?

Daniel Belavy: Well, of course because it's a cross-sectional study we can't be
100% certain, but we had a detailed look at the people's physical activity, and we
quantified that. And what we found is that it doesn't appear to be the actual
loading or the loading on the spine from running or from jogging, rather it looks
like it might even be in that walking loading phase or slow jogging activities.

Norman Swan: So you describe this as acceleration in the paper. So if you go
for a jog, certainly if you are me going for a jog, you're not jogging flat-out the
whole time, you've got to stop to cross the road, make a concession to motor
 
cars and things like that. So it's that slowing down, starting up that seems to
stress the spine and make the discs larger, is that what it is?

Daniel Belavy: That we can't say, not from the data. It looks like…I guess the
key message that came out of the further analyses is that it doesn't appear that
you have to go off and become a marathon on runners to get this effect. You
don't have to start jogging 40ks a week and keep doing it for five years. It looks
like…

Norman Swan: And it doesn't seem to matter whether you run on grass or
concrete.

Daniel Belavy: That probably doesn't matter too much for this kind of thing.
There is a lot of dampening of forces when you…you might feel more shock
forces in your lower leg if you are running on concrete, but by the time that gets
up to your spine that has been dampened a lot. I mean, we can't answer that
question here but…

Norman Swan: So you're still not absolutely sure what causes it, but it's certainly
not doing any harm, it does you some good. And does this inform back pain at
all?

Daniel Belavy: Yes, it does. The key thing about this finding for back pain is that
it helps us understand what kinds of physical activity are good for the spine. It's
one thing to avoid things we know are risky, but you want to be able to make
things better. And from the point of view of preventing back pain, I think this is
important for…you can treat back pain by going for a run, that's another issue.
It's important to keep active when you have back pain, it's very important, but I
view it as being very important for prevention to know what kinds of physical
activity do we need to do to have…to be treating our spines well and reduce the
risks of getting back problems.

Norman Swan: And do these 25- to 35-year-olds have clapped-out knees
because of their running?

Daniel Belavy: No, no.

Norman Swan: So that's another…
 
Daniel Belavy: I mean, obviously if you're going off and doing marathon running,
there is a risk of overuse injuries. But this was a healthy collective. They don't get
those…they weren't all wrecks in the lower legs because of that or anything like
that, no.

Norman Swan: Fascinating. Daniel, thank you, we look forward to your
randomised trial.

Daniel Belavy: Okay, thank you Norman.

Norman Swan: Daniel Belavy is an associate professor in the Institute of
Physical Activity and Nutrition at Deakin University in Melbourne.

And you're listening to the Health Report on RN, ABC news and CBC radio
across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

There have been suggestions in the past that populations of people with normal
or high normal vitamin D levels have lower rates of heart disease, and that has
made some experts argue that vitamin D supplements must be good for your
heart and arteries, rather than the alternate explanation which is that such people
might just be out in the sun, living a healthier lifestyle than the average person.
Anyway, there have been some randomised trials of relatively low dose vitamin D
which have not shown any protective effects, which is why a New Zealand group
has tested high doses. The lead researcher was Robert Scragg at the University
of Auckland. He is currently in London, which is where we have woken him up to
talk to you. Welcome to the Health Report, Robert.

Robert Scragg: Thank you, good morning Norman.

Norman Swan: Yes, I hope you've had your first cup of coffee. Tell us about this
study.

Robert Scragg: Well, the study started in 2011, over a couple of years we
recruited about 5,000 people, and then gave them monthly doses of vitamin D or
a very exactly similar looking placebo, and followed them up until the middle of
2015. So it's the largest study to date on high dose vitamin D…

Norman Swan: And it was 200,000 units you were giving them.
 
Robert Scragg: It was the initial bolus dose of 200,000, and then a monthly dose
that we mailed to their homes. So that's the equivalent to about 3,300
international unit a day, much more than what previous studies had used.

Norman Swan: And did they take the vitamin D?

Robert Scragg: Yes, from the evidence that we had from the study we had very
good adherence. There was a subgroup where we did measure their vitamin D
levels, and in that group we doubled the vitamin D levels in people that took
vitamin D. We also monitored that through questionnaires. And from the
questionnaires that we had returned to us we estimated that about 85% of
capsules were taken during the follow-up period, so very excellent adherence,
and also very good retention. In New Zealand here we can link everybody
through a unique number to Ministry of Health records on cardiovascular disease
and mortality. So in effect nobody dropped out of our study because we could
track what was happening to their health status.

Norman Swan: Yes, the New Zealanders always do it better than us. And these
were people aged over 50, average age 65. Were they at particularly high risk of
heart disease?

Robert Scragg: Well, they were in the high risk group, from 50 to 84. The
average age is about 66, 67 at baseline, so right across the…

Norman Swan: So they are at high risk just because of their age?

Robert Scragg: Because of their age. It turned out that, as happens in clinical
trials, they are healthier than average. So we didn't get the number of deaths that
we expected in this group, but this is pretty par for the course when it comes to
clinical trials.

Norman Swan: Dammit, people are living longer, it's just really annoying isn't it!
And what did you find?

Robert Scragg: Well, it was a little disappointing, having spent a huge amount of
effort on it, but basically we didn't find any effect whatsoever from vitamin D on
heart disease rates and stroke rates as well, right across the spectrum of
cardiovascular disease.
 
Norman Swan: I should have asked you that right at the beginning, so you were
looking at heart attack, stroke, heart failure, whether you needed a stent, that sort
of thing?

Robert Scragg: Yes, people with newly diagnosed hypertension. The full
spectrum of cardiovascular disease that the previous observational studies have
shown this inverse relationship with vitamin D status. So we didn't find anything
in our study. The effect was almost even in the two groups that we were
comparing, vitamin D and placebo. We even looked into low vitamin D levels and
didn't find any effect there either.

Norman Swan: So if you came in with low vitamin D levels, it didn't make a
difference. So, done deal, vitamin D doesn't help your heart?

Robert Scragg: No, no, it's not a done deal. There is emerging evidence to
suggest that daily supplements of vitamin D might be more beneficial for other
health effects like particularly respiratory infection. So I think we have to wait for
the other big studies underway at the moment, and particularly there is a large
study being carried out in the US called the Vital Study where they are giving
daily vitamin D. And also there is a very large study being carried out in Australia
called D Health being led by researchers from the University of Queensland. So I
think we need to wait for those studies to come in before we are 100% sure
what's going on with vitamin D and cardiovascular disease. There certainly is
evidence for other health benefits, so I think in another three or four years when
all the large studies currently underway are in, then we'll know what's going on
with this hormone.

Norman Swan: So don't sell your shares in the vitamin companies just yet.

Robert Scragg: Well, if I had any, I would hold onto them, but I don't.

Norman Swan: Robert, thanks very much for joining us, I'll let you get on with
your day in London.

Robert Scragg: Thank you very much Norman, bye bye.

Norman Swan: Robert Scragg is in the School of Population Health at the
University of Auckland.
 
Over 300,000 women give birth in Australia each year, and an astounding one in
five of their babies require resuscitation. I had to resuscitate one of my
daughters. And according to one of a series of papers in the Lancet this week, I'd
probably do it differently if it were today. Then there are the 9% of babies born
who are preterm, defined as being delivered earlier than 37 weeks gestation. The
average preterm baby in Australia is born at 33 weeks, and many require
intensive care, usually because of their immature lungs. And things have
changed there too in the last two or three decades, according to another in
this Lancet series.

But some things remain the same, such as the spectre of a dreadful chronic lung
condition called bronchopulmonary dysplasia, or BPD. Two of the Lancet authors
who are at the Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne join us now, Brett Manly
and Louise Owen, both of them are neonatologists. Welcome to you both.

Louise Owen: Thank you.

Brett Manley: Good evening Norman.

Norman Swan: Brett, let's start with the resuscitation, you were the lead author
on that paper. We used to be terrified when you had a baby with what's called
meconium aspiration where the baby had pooed in the womb and you breathed
in, and you'd run to it and suck the baby out. But from your paper, it turns out I
did it all wrong in my early days.

Brett Manley: Well, that might be right Norman. It seems, like a lot of areas in
neonatology, we've come full circle in our understanding of how to treat some
conditions of newborn babies, and meconium aspiration is one of them where we
have gone from suctioning all infants to try and get the meconium out of their
airways after they are born, to now minimising the infants that we suction the
meconium from.

Norman Swan: And that gives you a better outcome because it's traumatic, is
that what the story is?

Brett Manley: Well, it certainly doesn't give worse outcomes, and I think the less
we can do, the better. A lesson that we've learned is that we really should be just
 
getting on and helping these babies breathe and not spending too much time
trying to suction the meconium from the airways.

Norman Swan: Because a lot of this…I mean, we'll come to just a few of the
things that you do, we don't have a lot of time, but a few things you do now that
you didn't do before, but it used to be when you had to ventilate the baby and
get…ventilating the baby with a mask is the other thing, or intubate the baby,
you're suggesting now that you don't use oxygen, you use air.

Brett Manley: Yes, that's right. Through the history of neonatology, as
technologies have increased we've gone from having really no therapies to help
babies breathe where all we could give them was oxygen, through to now having
a lot better understanding of how we should help babies breathe, and also having
much better technologies. And as the years have gone by we've come to realise
that oxygen is not a benign drug, and actually babies that don't need as much
oxygen as we think they do, it can do harm.

Norman Swan: Such as?

Brett Manley: Well, the recommendations now in term babies are that actually
resuscitating babies in oxygen will improve survival…

Norman Swan: In air you mean?

Brett Manley: Sorry, in air, that's correct, in no oxygen. And in preterm infants
we have seen epidemics through history of oxygen diseases such as retinopathy
of prematurity, that's the blindness associated with too much oxygen.

Norman Swan: And even just in the labour ward, so a short episode of too much
oxygen can damage the eyes of these premature babies.

Brett Manley: It seems that way. And so now when we are resuscitating a sick
newborn infant, all term and late preterm babies will be resuscitated in air, that's
21% oxygen. The preterm infants we are still trying to work out the best way to
use oxygen, particularly the very preterm infants born before 32 weeks of
gestation. And it seems like those very preterm babies do need some oxygen.

Norman Swan: And delayed clamping of the umbilical cord?
 
Brett Manley: Well, another example of things going full circle in neonatology.
There's a long history describing delayed clamping of the cord, but in recent
decades it has been much more common for the cord to be clamped immediately
after birth. But now we are seeing the benefits of both for term and preterm
babies of delaying clamping of the cord, even by 60 seconds or more. And I think
that the potential benefits depend on whether babies are born in developed or
developing countries. For example, in developing countries, that little bit longer
with some more blood flowing towards the baby might increase iron stores and
help to reduce iron deficiency anaemia.

Norman Swan: And sometimes you can get a very oxygen deprived baby
coming out and you are very worried about the baby, and a natural inclination
with a newborn baby is to warm them, but in fact making them a bit cold
therapeutically is good for them if there's brain damage.

Brett Manley: Yes, I think a very important advance over the last decade or so
has been our use of therapeutic cooling, whole body cooling of babies who have
suffered birth asphyxia, who have been deprived of oxygen and blood to their
brain. And we've seen that particularly for those babies who are moderately to
severely affected, that this cooling for several days and keeping the core body
temperature low really does improve survival and other outcomes.

Norman Swan: Louise Owen, 'less is more' seems to be the theme in preterm
babies as well. What we've just been talking about with Brett is often the full term
baby needing resuscitation, but not exclusively, but in preterm babies the general
care seems to be less is more.

Louise Owen: I think so. As Brett has said, we've come a very long way in a very
short space of time, we've gone from doing nothing to doing everything, to then
actually the realisation that some of these things, they might just be a therapeutic
middle ground. So we've gone from being able to do nothing to using ventilators
on everybody, putting tubes into their airways, and then realising that perhaps
that isn't sensible for all babies, and there might be an easier way to support
them gently without further damaging their very delicate lungs.

Norman Swan: Such as?
 
Louise Owen: Such as just putting some short little prongs inside their nose and
using warmed gases that are humidified, with a little bit of additional oxygen if
required, and allowing them to breathe themselves. These babies are not born
without any drive to breathe, they can sometimes breathe very nicely on their
own with a little bit of support from us.

Norman Swan: And presumably you can make it worse with intubation?

Louise Owen: Absolutely we can. When we first saw the use of ventilation in
premature babies in the late '60s and early '70s, we thought it was a fantastic
thing to do, and babies did survive, but we did pay the price with damaging their
lungs and saw a big increase in the babies who had the chronic lung disease, the
bronchopulmonary dysplasia you mentioned earlier.

Norman Swan: And has that gone down over the years? Because in your paper
you imply that it's still pretty common and you're not quite sure how to prevent it.

Louise Owen: That's right, it unfortunately hasn't gone down…

Norman Swan: I should explain here, this ends up with a child who sometimes
requires oxygen for extended periods, doesn't have very good exercise capacity,
and really can limit the first few years of that child's life.

Louise Owen: That's right, it's a really important clinical condition, very important
for families and young children, but what we found is that we've actually seen the
rates rise over time, and part of that is because more of these babies are actually
surviving, and babies who may have had chronic lung disease historically would
have died and we never saw it, whereas now these babies survive. But they've
also had to live through all the things that we do to them and with them, for them,
trying to keep them alive but can also damage their lungs.

Norman Swan: And is less is more still true of extreme premature babies who
are 25, 26, 27 weeks?

Louise Owen: It is. We are still finding our way exactly how low we can go and
what the correct level is, but it does seem to be so, even for these tiny babies.

Norman Swan: What about other risks, and you don't mention this in your paper
because you are talking about the respiratory issues, but one thing that Brett
 
mentioned was this retinopathy, retrolental fibroplasia, where you basically can
get blindness because of oxygen therapy. What's the story now with oxygen
monitoring and trying to prevent this eye disease?

Louise Owen: That's a good question. We've come from not being able to do
anything except thinking a baby looked blue and giving them unrestricted
oxygen, through to now having lots of simple, non-invasive ways to measure
babies' oxygen. We've gone from giving them lots of oxygen, where babies
survived but lots went blind, through to the opposite where we restricted oxygen
and babies didn't go blind but more of them died because they had low oxygen
levels, to great big studies that have been done all around the world trying to find
the middle ground. And we are still working towards it. And the oxygen guidelines
are still changing, we are still tailoring that. But a little bit lower than adult level
seems to be about where we are aiming.

Norman Swan: Right. And brain damage, cerebral palsy, learning difficulties?

Louise Owen: These are still part of one of the things that we see in a very
preterm babies, and due to a whole multitude of factors, some of them from
before birth, some of them during their very prolonged stay in the newborn
intensive care units.

Norman Swan: And is 'less is more' giving you a better outcome intellectually in
terms of the brain function?

Louise Owen: I don't think we know that. It's very multifactorial. There are so
many things that play into that, lots of things that can or cannot happen to a
preterm baby after they are born. Does the baby have an episode of very low
oxygen, does the baby have an episode of bad infection, of sepsis? So many
things play into that over the time, it's hard to be more specific.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much to you both, fascinating and important
news. Louise Owen and Brett Manly are consultant neonatologists at the Royal
Women's Hospital in Melbourne.

Cancer of the uterus, the technical term is endometrial cancer, is the commonest
gynaecological cancer and it's becoming more common in association with the
rise in obesity in the community. The treatment is surgical with the removal of the
 
uterus, hysterectomy, and the tubes and ovaries, plus any involved lymph nodes,
and that can be done in two main ways; an open operation via a large incision or
a largish incision, or keyhole surgery using laparoscopy, the telescope. And while
laparoscopic surgery for uterine cancer has taken off, there are lingering doubts
about whether it catches all the tumour and whether the complications are
problematic.

Randomised trials are not very common in surgery, but to the great credit of a
consortium of gynaecological oncologists across Australia and New Zealand, a
trial comparing total abdominal hysterectomy with laparoscopy looking at
disease-free survival has recently been published. One of the organisers was
Andreas Obermair of the Queensland Centre for Gynaecological Cancer at the
Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital, and Andreas is in our Brisbane studio.
Welcome to the Health Report.

Andreas Obermair: Hello Norman.

Norman Swan: So this was early uterine cancer you were looking at?

Andreas Obermair: Yes, that's right.

Norman Swan: What is early uterine cancer? There's a bit of controversy about
that, isn't there?

Andreas Obermair: Well, we believe that about 80% of all uterine cancers are
non-aggressive and are early…we basically define early as the disease is
confined to the uterus.

Norman Swan: So tell us about this trial.

Andreas Obermair: Well, we started this trial approximately 15 years ago,
designing it…

Norman Swan: 15 years ago!

Andreas Obermair: That's the life cycle of a surgical clinical trial with follow-up
of four and a half years. We started this trial at the Queensland Centre for
Gynaecological Cancer with private donations because we couldn't get funding
for this trial. There certainly wasn't government funding available. We employed
 
our first research nurse and collected data, and with these data we then were
able to apply for funding. And the funding basically made certain that we could
see this through and continue this trial until we had the very first results available.
And as you are aware, the very first results were very, very good, they were very
encouraging. They have shown that patients mobilised better, their quality of life
is better. Then we published data on complication…

Norman Swan: So this is abdominal versus laparoscopic. So the quality of life
was better, but the key was whether or not you treated the disease well.

Andreas Obermair: We were dumbfounded by how much better laparoscopic
surgery was. We had an idea that keyhole surgery was better but we were
amazed by the extent of how better it was. But there was always, as you say,
these lingering doubts, whether keyhole surgery would cause early recurrences,
and that really wasn't known. And the paper that we published recently is
basically really good news for patients with endometrial cancer, saying there is
no trade-off. It continues to be good news, there is no compromise in survival
outcomes or in recurrences.

Norman Swan: And what proportion of women reverted to the open operation
when you did the laparoscopic, so they ended up with the open operation
anyway?

Andreas Obermair: That was very minor, between 6% and 10%. I should say in
fairness, there is a study, a sister study has been done in the United States and
they had a larger conversion rate…

Norman Swan: They're not as good there, you know!

Andreas Obermair: No, no, that wasn't the point, but the point was that they had
to do aortic node dissection, and in really big women that is very, very difficult,
and I think that cannot be achieved laparoscopically.

Norman Swan: So in other words if you go in and you find that it's not early, you
probably do have to revert to an open operation to get the lymph nodes out well.
 
Andreas Obermair: Well, as a matter of fact we try to stay with laparoscopic
surgery, but yes, there are certain situations where you just can't push on
laparoscopically, that's right.

Norman Swan: And what about complications that keep gynaecological
oncologists up at night, such as pranging the ureter, which is the tube that comes
down from the kidneys to the bladder?

Andreas Obermair: Well, that was also very interesting because previous
research suggested that intraoperative complications such as pranging the ureter
or blood vessels or bladder or the bowel is more common, which was not the
case in our study. So in our study there was not an increased risk. The risk of
complications was exactly the same intraoperatively. However, what we also
found, that post-operative complications were far less in the laparoscopic arm.
So down to 50%.

Norman Swan: So the message for women is find a gynaecological oncologist
who does the keyhole surgery? Or is that now pretty universal in Australia?

Andreas Obermair: Well, in gynaecological oncology I think most
gynaecological cancer units would offer laparoscopic hysterectomy, but you are
right, I think women need to be educated that laparoscopic surgery is available,
and they shouldn't settle for a total abdominal hysterectomy.

Norman Swan: Andreas, thanks for joining us on the Health Report.

Andreas Obermair: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Andreas Obermair is in the Queensland Centre for
Gynaecological Cancer at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital.

I'm Norman Swan, you've been with the Health Report, try and join us next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, vitamin D supplements and your heart. Another win for
keyhole surgery in women. How things are changing in the resuscitation of
newborn babies in the labour ward, and also in the care of preterm babies. And
jogging and your back.

Most people will suffer an episode of back pain some time in their lives, often
more than one. It's a huge cause of lost days at work and medical costs, not to
mention the disability that can be involved. You can find experts who say that
jogging is poison for the back because it pummels the spine. But a world first
study from Deakin University on the effects of jogging and running on
intervertebral discs suggests otherwise. The lead author is Daniel Belavy and
he's in our Melbourne studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Daniel Belavy: Good evening Norman.

Norman Swan: So tell us about this study.

Daniel Belavy: Well, as you introduced, back pain is a massive problem for
Australian society, and it's the leading cause of disability and lost productivity in
the country, even when you account for more deaths due to other diseases. And
in managing this sort of issue, what I wanted to look at was to see can we find
ways to, for example, strengthen the discs in the back. And the conventional
wisdom in the research field is that either you can't or if there is an effect, that it's
going to be too slow to have a meaningful effect in a person's life.

Norman Swan: And whilst there was some evidence in animals, there was no
evidence in humans that exercise did make a difference.

Daniel Belavy: Precisely, and the thing is that what might happen or be relevant
in an animal mightn't be the case in humans because…

Norman Swan: And we're talking about the shock absorbers between the
vertebra, the bones in the spine.

Daniel Belavy: Precisely, yes, and as you said, this research has been done
with animals before, but their metabolism is a lot faster and also they walk on all
fours. And whether that applies then to humans is another matter.

Norman Swan: So tell us what you did in the study?

Daniel Belavy: Well, what I decided to do is to look at certain kinds of physical
activity that we think are possibly going to be at the very worst not detrimental to
the spine at high volumes, or they might be beneficial. Based upon the work from
animals and also from other studies we've seen before, I thought that examining
walking or running might be a good way to see if this exercise can actually
improve the discs.

Norman Swan: So you have three groups of relatively young people, 25, 35,
men and women, with varying levels of activity. Tell us about their varying levels
of activity.

Daniel Belavy: Well, we had obviously a group of people who didn't do any sport
at all, they were healthy, they had no back problems at all, but they just were
simply not involved in any regular physical activity. And then we had a group of
people who regularly run marathons, so running at least 50 kilometres a week
and doing that for at least five years. And also a group of people who were
regular joggers, so running 20 to 40 kilometres a week, and also for at least five
years, but also, again, no other kind of sports. We just looked at people who just
ran. So triathletes and so forth we didn't look at.

Norman Swan: And you did MRIs on their backs?

Daniel Belavy: Yes.

Norman Swan: What did you find? So this is not a randomised trial, this is just
seeing what the effect was.

Daniel Belavy: Just seeing what the effect was, because there is no data in
humans, before you go off and do the randomised controlled trial you need to
see if there is any kind of effect at all, and back in the studies on bone in the late
'80s and early '90s you needed that first cross-sectional study between different
types of sports or different types of athletic groups to see if there was a
difference, and that was then the justification to say, okay, let's go off and do a
randomised controlled trial.

Norman Swan: So what did you find about their discs?

Daniel Belavy: Well, we found that the runners had better discs. And most
interestingly, on the one hand we found there was more water and more
hydration in the disc, and that's an indicator of a healthier disc. And we also
found in the marathon runners, and I was personally really, really surprised about
this finding, that their discs were actually bigger. Compared to the size of their
bones in the spine, the discs were a lot bigger, and that's an indicator that the
discs actually got bigger in response to the loading.

Norman Swan: And this is controlled for because your muscles around the spine
are going to be stronger and so on…

Daniel Belavy: Well, not necessarily, the muscles, actually there was no
difference between the different groups in their muscle size.

Norman Swan: And so this is a pure effect on…but I thought there wasn't that
much difference between the joggers and the long distance runners?

Daniel Belavy: There wasn't much of a difference between the two, that's true,
and that did surprise me a little bit, I thought we might see a stepwise effect, but
looking at the data further, it seemed like…sometimes you hit a ceiling with how
much of a response you can get from a tissue. Like, you can do muscle training
as much as you want, you only get so far, no matter how much you train your
muscle, it won't keep on expanding and keep on getting bigger.

Norman Swan: So why this effect then? So basically healthier, larger discs with
jogging and running, and 150 minutes a week I think is what you said with the
jogging roughly. So what was causing it? Was it the impact or what?

Daniel Belavy: Well, of course because it's a cross-sectional study we can't be
100% certain, but we had a detailed look at the people's physical activity, and we
quantified that. And what we found is that it doesn't appear to be the actual
loading or the loading on the spine from running or from jogging, rather it looks
like it might even be in that walking loading phase or slow jogging activities.

Norman Swan: So you describe this as acceleration in the paper. So if you go
for a jog, certainly if you are me going for a jog, you're not jogging flat-out the
whole time, you've got to stop to cross the road, make a concession to motor

cars and things like that. So it's that slowing down, starting up that seems to
stress the spine and make the discs larger, is that what it is?

Daniel Belavy: That we can't say, not from the data. It looks like…I guess the
key message that came out of the further analyses is that it doesn't appear that
you have to go off and become a marathon on runners to get this effect. You
don't have to start jogging 40ks a week and keep doing it for five years. It looks
like…

Norman Swan: And it doesn't seem to matter whether you run on grass or
concrete.

Daniel Belavy: That probably doesn't matter too much for this kind of thing.
There is a lot of dampening of forces when you…you might feel more shock
forces in your lower leg if you are running on concrete, but by the time that gets
up to your spine that has been dampened a lot. I mean, we can't answer that
question here but…

Norman Swan: So you're still not absolutely sure what causes it, but it's certainly
not doing any harm, it does you some good. And does this inform back pain at
all?

Daniel Belavy: Yes, it does. The key thing about this finding for back pain is that
it helps us understand what kinds of physical activity are good for the spine. It's
one thing to avoid things we know are risky, but you want to be able to make
things better. And from the point of view of preventing back pain, I think this is
important for…you can treat back pain by going for a run, that's another issue.
It's important to keep active when you have back pain, it's very important, but I
view it as being very important for prevention to know what kinds of physical
activity do we need to do to have…to be treating our spines well and reduce the
risks of getting back problems.

Norman Swan: And do these 25- to 35-year-olds have clapped-out knees
because of their running?

Daniel Belavy: No, no.

Norman Swan: So that's another…

Daniel Belavy: I mean, obviously if you're going off and doing marathon running,
there is a risk of overuse injuries. But this was a healthy collective. They don't get
those…they weren't all wrecks in the lower legs because of that or anything like
that, no.

Norman Swan: Fascinating. Daniel, thank you, we look forward to your
randomised trial.

Daniel Belavy: Okay, thank you Norman.

Norman Swan: Daniel Belavy is an associate professor in the Institute of
Physical Activity and Nutrition at Deakin University in Melbourne.

And you're listening to the Health Report on RN, ABC news and CBC radio
across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

There have been suggestions in the past that populations of people with normal
or high normal vitamin D levels have lower rates of heart disease, and that has
made some experts argue that vitamin D supplements must be good for your
heart and arteries, rather than the alternate explanation which is that such people
might just be out in the sun, living a healthier lifestyle than the average person.
Anyway, there have been some randomised trials of relatively low dose vitamin D
which have not shown any protective effects, which is why a New Zealand group
has tested high doses. The lead researcher was Robert Scragg at the University
of Auckland. He is currently in London, which is where we have woken him up to
talk to you. Welcome to the Health Report, Robert.

Robert Scragg: Thank you, good morning Norman.

Norman Swan: Yes, I hope you've had your first cup of coffee. Tell us about this
study.

Robert Scragg: Well, the study started in 2011, over a couple of years we
recruited about 5,000 people, and then gave them monthly doses of vitamin D or
a very exactly similar looking placebo, and followed them up until the middle of
2015. So it's the largest study to date on high dose vitamin D…

Norman Swan: And it was 200,000 units you were giving them.

Robert Scragg: It was the initial bolus dose of 200,000, and then a monthly dose
that we mailed to their homes. So that's the equivalent to about 3,300
international unit a day, much more than what previous studies had used.

Norman Swan: And did they take the vitamin D?

Robert Scragg: Yes, from the evidence that we had from the study we had very
good adherence. There was a subgroup where we did measure their vitamin D
levels, and in that group we doubled the vitamin D levels in people that took
vitamin D. We also monitored that through questionnaires. And from the
questionnaires that we had returned to us we estimated that about 85% of
capsules were taken during the follow-up period, so very excellent adherence,
and also very good retention. In New Zealand here we can link everybody
through a unique number to Ministry of Health records on cardiovascular disease
and mortality. So in effect nobody dropped out of our study because we could
track what was happening to their health status.

Norman Swan: Yes, the New Zealanders always do it better than us. And these
were people aged over 50, average age 65. Were they at particularly high risk of
heart disease?

Robert Scragg: Well, they were in the high risk group, from 50 to 84. The
average age is about 66, 67 at baseline, so right across the…

Norman Swan: So they are at high risk just because of their age?

Robert Scragg: Because of their age. It turned out that, as happens in clinical
trials, they are healthier than average. So we didn't get the number of deaths that
we expected in this group, but this is pretty par for the course when it comes to
clinical trials.

Norman Swan: Dammit, people are living longer, it's just really annoying isn't it!
And what did you find?

Robert Scragg: Well, it was a little disappointing, having spent a huge amount of
effort on it, but basically we didn't find any effect whatsoever from vitamin D on
heart disease rates and stroke rates as well, right across the spectrum of
cardiovascular disease.

Norman Swan: I should have asked you that right at the beginning, so you were
looking at heart attack, stroke, heart failure, whether you needed a stent, that sort
of thing?

Robert Scragg: Yes, people with newly diagnosed hypertension. The full
spectrum of cardiovascular disease that the previous observational studies have
shown this inverse relationship with vitamin D status. So we didn't find anything
in our study. The effect was almost even in the two groups that we were
comparing, vitamin D and placebo. We even looked into low vitamin D levels and
didn't find any effect there either.

Norman Swan: So if you came in with low vitamin D levels, it didn't make a
difference. So, done deal, vitamin D doesn't help your heart?

Robert Scragg: No, no, it's not a done deal. There is emerging evidence to
suggest that daily supplements of vitamin D might be more beneficial for other
health effects like particularly respiratory infection. So I think we have to wait for
the other big studies underway at the moment, and particularly there is a large
study being carried out in the US called the Vital Study where they are giving
daily vitamin D. And also there is a very large study being carried out in Australia
called D Health being led by researchers from the University of Queensland. So I
think we need to wait for those studies to come in before we are 100% sure
what's going on with vitamin D and cardiovascular disease. There certainly is
evidence for other health benefits, so I think in another three or four years when
all the large studies currently underway are in, then we'll know what's going on
with this hormone.

Norman Swan: So don't sell your shares in the vitamin companies just yet.

Robert Scragg: Well, if I had any, I would hold onto them, but I don't.

Norman Swan: Robert, thanks very much for joining us, I'll let you get on with
your day in London.

Robert Scragg: Thank you very much Norman, bye bye.

Norman Swan: Robert Scragg is in the School of Population Health at the
University of Auckland.

Over 300,000 women give birth in Australia each year, and an astounding one in
five of their babies require resuscitation. I had to resuscitate one of my
daughters. And according to one of a series of papers in the Lancet this week, I'd
probably do it differently if it were today. Then there are the 9% of babies born
who are preterm, defined as being delivered earlier than 37 weeks gestation. The
average preterm baby in Australia is born at 33 weeks, and many require
intensive care, usually because of their immature lungs. And things have
changed there too in the last two or three decades, according to another in
this Lancet series.

But some things remain the same, such as the spectre of a dreadful chronic lung
condition called bronchopulmonary dysplasia, or BPD. Two of the Lancet authors
who are at the Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne join us now, Brett Manly
and Louise Owen, both of them are neonatologists. Welcome to you both.

Louise Owen: Thank you.

Brett Manley: Good evening Norman.

Norman Swan: Brett, let's start with the resuscitation, you were the lead author
on that paper. We used to be terrified when you had a baby with what's called
meconium aspiration where the baby had pooed in the womb and you breathed
in, and you'd run to it and suck the baby out. But from your paper, it turns out I
did it all wrong in my early days.

Brett Manley: Well, that might be right Norman. It seems, like a lot of areas in
neonatology, we've come full circle in our understanding of how to treat some
conditions of newborn babies, and meconium aspiration is one of them where we
have gone from suctioning all infants to try and get the meconium out of their
airways after they are born, to now minimising the infants that we suction the
meconium from.

Norman Swan: And that gives you a better outcome because it's traumatic, is
that what the story is?

Brett Manley: Well, it certainly doesn't give worse outcomes, and I think the less
we can do, the better. A lesson that we've learned is that we really should be just

getting on and helping these babies breathe and not spending too much time
trying to suction the meconium from the airways.

Norman Swan: Because a lot of this…I mean, we'll come to just a few of the
things that you do, we don't have a lot of time, but a few things you do now that
you didn't do before, but it used to be when you had to ventilate the baby and
get…ventilating the baby with a mask is the other thing, or intubate the baby,
you're suggesting now that you don't use oxygen, you use air.

Brett Manley: Yes, that's right. Through the history of neonatology, as
technologies have increased we've gone from having really no therapies to help
babies breathe where all we could give them was oxygen, through to now having
a lot better understanding of how we should help babies breathe, and also having
much better technologies. And as the years have gone by we've come to realise
that oxygen is not a benign drug, and actually babies that don't need as much
oxygen as we think they do, it can do harm.

Norman Swan: Such as?

Brett Manley: Well, the recommendations now in term babies are that actually
resuscitating babies in oxygen will improve survival…

Norman Swan: In air you mean?

Brett Manley: Sorry, in air, that's correct, in no oxygen. And in preterm infants
we have seen epidemics through history of oxygen diseases such as retinopathy
of prematurity, that's the blindness associated with too much oxygen.

Norman Swan: And even just in the labour ward, so a short episode of too much
oxygen can damage the eyes of these premature babies.

Brett Manley: It seems that way. And so now when we are resuscitating a sick
newborn infant, all term and late preterm babies will be resuscitated in air, that's
21% oxygen. The preterm infants we are still trying to work out the best way to
use oxygen, particularly the very preterm infants born before 32 weeks of
gestation. And it seems like those very preterm babies do need some oxygen.

Norman Swan: And delayed clamping of the umbilical cord?

Brett Manley: Well, another example of things going full circle in neonatology.
There's a long history describing delayed clamping of the cord, but in recent
decades it has been much more common for the cord to be clamped immediately
after birth. But now we are seeing the benefits of both for term and preterm
babies of delaying clamping of the cord, even by 60 seconds or more. And I think
that the potential benefits depend on whether babies are born in developed or
developing countries. For example, in developing countries, that little bit longer
with some more blood flowing towards the baby might increase iron stores and
help to reduce iron deficiency anaemia.

Norman Swan: And sometimes you can get a very oxygen deprived baby
coming out and you are very worried about the baby, and a natural inclination
with a newborn baby is to warm them, but in fact making them a bit cold
therapeutically is good for them if there's brain damage.

Brett Manley: Yes, I think a very important advance over the last decade or so
has been our use of therapeutic cooling, whole body cooling of babies who have
suffered birth asphyxia, who have been deprived of oxygen and blood to their
brain. And we've seen that particularly for those babies who are moderately to
severely affected, that this cooling for several days and keeping the core body
temperature low really does improve survival and other outcomes.

Norman Swan: Louise Owen, 'less is more' seems to be the theme in preterm
babies as well. What we've just been talking about with Brett is often the full term
baby needing resuscitation, but not exclusively, but in preterm babies the general
care seems to be less is more.

Louise Owen: I think so. As Brett has said, we've come a very long way in a very
short space of time, we've gone from doing nothing to doing everything, to then
actually the realisation that some of these things, they might just be a therapeutic
middle ground. So we've gone from being able to do nothing to using ventilators
on everybody, putting tubes into their airways, and then realising that perhaps
that isn't sensible for all babies, and there might be an easier way to support
them gently without further damaging their very delicate lungs.

Norman Swan: Such as?

Louise Owen: Such as just putting some short little prongs inside their nose and
using warmed gases that are humidified, with a little bit of additional oxygen if
required, and allowing them to breathe themselves. These babies are not born
without any drive to breathe, they can sometimes breathe very nicely on their
own with a little bit of support from us.

Norman Swan: And presumably you can make it worse with intubation?

Louise Owen: Absolutely we can. When we first saw the use of ventilation in
premature babies in the late '60s and early '70s, we thought it was a fantastic
thing to do, and babies did survive, but we did pay the price with damaging their
lungs and saw a big increase in the babies who had the chronic lung disease, the
bronchopulmonary dysplasia you mentioned earlier.

Norman Swan: And has that gone down over the years? Because in your paper
you imply that it's still pretty common and you're not quite sure how to prevent it.

Louise Owen: That's right, it unfortunately hasn't gone down…

Norman Swan: I should explain here, this ends up with a child who sometimes
requires oxygen for extended periods, doesn't have very good exercise capacity,
and really can limit the first few years of that child's life.

Louise Owen: That's right, it's a really important clinical condition, very important
for families and young children, but what we found is that we've actually seen the
rates rise over time, and part of that is because more of these babies are actually
surviving, and babies who may have had chronic lung disease historically would
have died and we never saw it, whereas now these babies survive. But they've
also had to live through all the things that we do to them and with them, for them,
trying to keep them alive but can also damage their lungs.

Norman Swan: And is less is more still true of extreme premature babies who
are 25, 26, 27 weeks?

Louise Owen: It is. We are still finding our way exactly how low we can go and
what the correct level is, but it does seem to be so, even for these tiny babies.

Norman Swan: What about other risks, and you don't mention this in your paper
because you are talking about the respiratory issues, but one thing that Brett

mentioned was this retinopathy, retrolental fibroplasia, where you basically can
get blindness because of oxygen therapy. What's the story now with oxygen
monitoring and trying to prevent this eye disease?

Louise Owen: That's a good question. We've come from not being able to do
anything except thinking a baby looked blue and giving them unrestricted
oxygen, through to now having lots of simple, non-invasive ways to measure
babies' oxygen. We've gone from giving them lots of oxygen, where babies
survived but lots went blind, through to the opposite where we restricted oxygen
and babies didn't go blind but more of them died because they had low oxygen
levels, to great big studies that have been done all around the world trying to find
the middle ground. And we are still working towards it. And the oxygen guidelines
are still changing, we are still tailoring that. But a little bit lower than adult level
seems to be about where we are aiming.

Norman Swan: Right. And brain damage, cerebral palsy, learning difficulties?

Louise Owen: These are still part of one of the things that we see in a very
preterm babies, and due to a whole multitude of factors, some of them from
before birth, some of them during their very prolonged stay in the newborn
intensive care units.

Norman Swan: And is 'less is more' giving you a better outcome intellectually in
terms of the brain function?

Louise Owen: I don't think we know that. It's very multifactorial. There are so
many things that play into that, lots of things that can or cannot happen to a
preterm baby after they are born. Does the baby have an episode of very low
oxygen, does the baby have an episode of bad infection, of sepsis? So many
things play into that over the time, it's hard to be more specific.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much to you both, fascinating and important
news. Louise Owen and Brett Manly are consultant neonatologists at the Royal
Women's Hospital in Melbourne.

Cancer of the uterus, the technical term is endometrial cancer, is the commonest
gynaecological cancer and it's becoming more common in association with the
rise in obesity in the community. The treatment is surgical with the removal of the

uterus, hysterectomy, and the tubes and ovaries, plus any involved lymph nodes,
and that can be done in two main ways; an open operation via a large incision or
a largish incision, or keyhole surgery using laparoscopy, the telescope. And while
laparoscopic surgery for uterine cancer has taken off, there are lingering doubts
about whether it catches all the tumour and whether the complications are
problematic.

Randomised trials are not very common in surgery, but to the great credit of a
consortium of gynaecological oncologists across Australia and New Zealand, a
trial comparing total abdominal hysterectomy with laparoscopy looking at
disease-free survival has recently been published. One of the organisers was
Andreas Obermair of the Queensland Centre for Gynaecological Cancer at the
Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital, and Andreas is in our Brisbane studio.
Welcome to the Health Report.

Andreas Obermair: Hello Norman.

Norman Swan: So this was early uterine cancer you were looking at?

Andreas Obermair: Yes, that's right.

Norman Swan: What is early uterine cancer? There's a bit of controversy about
that, isn't there?

Andreas Obermair: Well, we believe that about 80% of all uterine cancers are
non-aggressive and are early…we basically define early as the disease is
confined to the uterus.

Norman Swan: So tell us about this trial.

Andreas Obermair: Well, we started this trial approximately 15 years ago,
designing it…

Norman Swan: 15 years ago!

Andreas Obermair: That's the life cycle of a surgical clinical trial with follow-up
of four and a half years. We started this trial at the Queensland Centre for
Gynaecological Cancer with private donations because we couldn't get funding
for this trial. There certainly wasn't government funding available. We employed

our first research nurse and collected data, and with these data we then were
able to apply for funding. And the funding basically made certain that we could
see this through and continue this trial until we had the very first results available.
And as you are aware, the very first results were very, very good, they were very
encouraging. They have shown that patients mobilised better, their quality of life
is better. Then we published data on complication…

Norman Swan: So this is abdominal versus laparoscopic. So the quality of life
was better, but the key was whether or not you treated the disease well.

Andreas Obermair: We were dumbfounded by how much better laparoscopic
surgery was. We had an idea that keyhole surgery was better but we were
amazed by the extent of how better it was. But there was always, as you say,
these lingering doubts, whether keyhole surgery would cause early recurrences,
and that really wasn't known. And the paper that we published recently is
basically really good news for patients with endometrial cancer, saying there is
no trade-off. It continues to be good news, there is no compromise in survival
outcomes or in recurrences.

Norman Swan: And what proportion of women reverted to the open operation
when you did the laparoscopic, so they ended up with the open operation
anyway?

Andreas Obermair: That was very minor, between 6% and 10%. I should say in
fairness, there is a study, a sister study has been done in the United States and
they had a larger conversion rate…

Norman Swan: They're not as good there, you know!

Andreas Obermair: No, no, that wasn't the point, but the point was that they had
to do aortic node dissection, and in really big women that is very, very difficult,
and I think that cannot be achieved laparoscopically.

Norman Swan: So in other words if you go in and you find that it's not early, you
probably do have to revert to an open operation to get the lymph nodes out well.

Andreas Obermair: Well, as a matter of fact we try to stay with laparoscopic
surgery, but yes, there are certain situations where you just can't push on
laparoscopically, that's right.

Norman Swan: And what about complications that keep gynaecological
oncologists up at night, such as pranging the ureter, which is the tube that comes
down from the kidneys to the bladder?

Andreas Obermair: Well, that was also very interesting because previous
research suggested that intraoperative complications such as pranging the ureter
or blood vessels or bladder or the bowel is more common, which was not the
case in our study. So in our study there was not an increased risk. The risk of
complications was exactly the same intraoperatively. However, what we also
found, that post-operative complications were far less in the laparoscopic arm.
So down to 50%.

Norman Swan: So the message for women is find a gynaecological oncologist
who does the keyhole surgery? Or is that now pretty universal in Australia?

Andreas Obermair: Well, in gynaecological oncology I think most
gynaecological cancer units would offer laparoscopic hysterectomy, but you are
right, I think women need to be educated that laparoscopic surgery is available,
and they shouldn't settle for a total abdominal hysterectomy.

Norman Swan: Andreas, thanks for joining us on the Health Report.

Andreas Obermair: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Andreas Obermair is in the Queensland Centre for
Gynaecological Cancer at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital.

I'm Norman Swan, you've been with the Health Report, try and join us next week.
